title: 72-hour emergency kit
tldr: Start with at least three days of safe water, ready-to-eat food, essential medicines, lighting and communication supplies. Include one gallon of water per person per day as a starting point, and account for pets, heat, medical needs and accessibility.
steps: Gather usable supplies before buying duplicates.
Choose safe water, shelf-stable food, a can opener, light, radio, batteries and phone charging.
Add medication arrangements, eyeglasses, infant needs, pet supplies, hygiene and accessible equipment.
Label dates, rotate food and water as instructed and check supplies routinely.
next: Build longer-duration supplies as space and budget allow. Keep an evacuation bag separate enough to carry.
watch: A standard checklist is only a starting point; three days may not cover a prolonged disruption.
shopping: Shelf-stable food and manual can opener
Pet and infant supplies as needed
review_status: source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
without_help: If shops close today, inventory water, shelf-stable food, medicine and batteries already at home. Put them together and write down gaps. Build a usable kit in stages; a partly stocked kit is more useful than waiting for an expensive perfect one.
household: Start with the people in the home: drinking water, medicines, infant feeding, sensory access, safe light and pet care. Choose who will carry shared items. A 72-hour kit is a planning starting point, not a guarantee that a disruption ends after three days.
pack_now: Prioritize supplies named in this guide that are usable by the person who needs them. Keep the checklist and relevant contact details accessible. Check carrying capacity, storage and equipment instructions in advance; collecting equipment must not delay the immediate protective action.

When the first option is unavailable

If shops close today, inventory water, shelf-stable food, medicine and batteries already at home. Put them together and write down gaps. Build a usable kit in stages; a partly stocked kit is more useful than waiting for an expensive perfect one.
faqs: How much can the household carry?

Separate supplies stored at home from a bag intended for evacuation. Test carrying the bag with the actual caregiver and mobility needs. Heavy water and duplicate tools can make a complete-looking kit unusable when movement matters.

Use normal household rotation where suitable and record refill dates. Check battery and device compatibility before relying on them. Medicine quantities and replacements require a clinician or pharmacist rather than an improvised rationing plan.
scope: Civilian educational guidance. Linked references may use U.S. emergency systems; local warning methods, laws, services and conditions differ.
